newsitem.title: USA: Oil, wheat, gold prices rise in U.S. trading.
newsitem.headline: Oil, wheat, gold prices rise in U.S. trading.

text.p: Supply concerns pushed oil and wheat prices higher Wednesday and precious metals prices also rose as optimism about mining company shares grew.
The gains helped boost the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures contracts up 1.84 points to 242.33.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil and product prices shot higher on the outlook for cold weather this week in the Northeast.

Heating oil for December delivery settled up 2.95 cents at 71.20 cents a gallon, December unleaded gasoline rose 2.57 cents to 68.34 cents a gallon and December crude oil rose 77 cents at $24.12 a barrel.
Temperatures this week were expected to be unseasonably cold in the Northeast, ranging about 11 to 15 degrees below normal. The region is the world's largest heating oil market.
Traders were worried that historically low heating oil stocks that have only recently begun to build up could be tapped too quickly by the cold snap.
"The rally in heating oil was driven by two factors, cold temperatures here and abroad and the possibility of a draw in stocks," said Prudential Securities trader Nauman Barakat.
The American Petroleum Institute said after the market closed that U.S. distillate stocks, which include heating oil, fell 827,000 barrels in the week ended on Nov. 8.
Crude oil stocks fell 6.61 million barrels and gasoline stocks 2.89 million barrels, more evidence that cold weather has rapidly increased oil consumption.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices rose for a second straight day as export prospects brightened. December wheat closed 9-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $4.00-3/4.

Traders said the market reacted to a flurry of fresh export interest following a monthly U.S. Agriculture Department report on Tuesday that trimmed the official estimate for U.S. and world wheat stocks next year.

The report said U.S. wheat stockpiles would total only 435 million bushels next June 1, down from 470 million seen a month earlier. Projected world stocks were cut to 110.8 million metric tons from 116.5 million a month earlier.
"It started yesterday with the cut in ending stocks and world production numbers plus there is talk Egypt will be in for wheat," said analyst Ron Kucha of O'Connor & Co.
Egypt was rumoured to be looking for 250,000 to 300,000 tons of wheat, Philippines bought 40,000 tons of U.S. wheat on Wednesday, and Taiwan was due to buy 80,000 tons on Thursday.

Traders also took note of Agriculture Department Secretary Dan Glickman's statement at the World Food Summit in Rome that U.S. use of grain export subsidies were an option if if the European Union continued its own subsidies.
The strong gains in wheat carried over to other CBOT pits, with December corn closing up 3-3/4 cents at $2.71-3/4 a bushel and November soybeans up 4-1/4 cents at $6.92-3/4.

Precious metals ended mostly higher for a fifth straight session, helped by sharp gains in mining stocks in the Philadelphia Stock Exchange's gold and silver stock index and related options, traders said.
December gold on the COMEX division of the New York Mercantile Exchange closed up 80 cents at $384.20 an ounce. December silver ended up 1.8 cents at $4.90 an ounce.

More big investment funds were buying "but I don't think you can ignore the move in the mining stocks, which have been looking undervalued by comparison with the rest of the stock market," Linnco Futures Group trader Anthony Raia said.

The Philadelphia Stock Exchange's gold and silver sector index was up 1.18 points near the close at 127.25, after seeing a 10-week high intraday at 129.63. The index is recovering from a 12-month low of 113.44 established Nov. 6.
January platinum fell 40 cents to $391.60 an ounce but December palladium rose $3.65 to $123.50 an ounce, its highest since mid-September.

On Tuesday, Johnson Matthey, the world's largest refiner of platinum group metals, forecast the supply of palladium would be 130,000 ounces short of demand this year compared with a surplus last year of 240,000 ounces.
